READING PASSAGE 3: Two Views of Pocket Parks
PASSAGE A
A pocket park occupies only a small lot, sometimes the footprint of a single demolished building. Its scale is often treated as a weakness: a few benches and trees cannot provide a playing field or a long walking path. Yet scale can also be the park’s advantage. Because a pocket park is inserted directly into a block, it can place shade, seating, and plant life within a short walk of residents who may not reach a large park often.

Designers should begin with repeated observation. A beautiful plan may fail if it ignores the hour when an adjacent restaurant needs deliveries or the path students take after school. Movable chairs, durable planting beds, and one clear open area can support several uses without pretending that the lot is larger than it is. Success should be measured locally: Are people staying longer on the block? Do older residents have a comfortable place to rest? Does rain soak into soil instead of rushing into a drain?

PASSAGE B
The enthusiasm for pocket parks sometimes outruns the evidence used to justify them. A photograph of a crowded opening day says little about use six months later. A city may celebrate a tiny new park while postponing maintenance at larger parks that serve far more people. Small sites also create a tempting illusion of low cost. The land may be donated, but irrigation, trash collection, lighting, and repairs continue every year.

This does not mean that small parks are a mistake. It means that cities should compare them with other investments. A shaded bus stop, a safer crossing, or grants for existing courtyards may offer more benefit on some blocks. Before choosing a pocket park, planners should state the problem they intend to solve and collect evidence after the ribbon is cut. A site that remains useful deserves support; one that does not should teach the city to choose differently next time.

Passage B also cautions against choosing measures only after a project opens. If planners celebrate whichever number improves, almost any site can be called successful. A stronger evaluation names a few outcomes in advance, records conditions before construction, and checks whether benefits persist across seasons. Those steps need not turn a small park into a research laboratory. They simply connect public claims to observations that residents and officials can examine.

Under that standard, the local questions favored by Passage A become especially useful. Shade, rest, drainage, and time spent on the block can all be observed at a scale appropriate to the site. The disagreement is therefore less about whether small parks can help than about what should happen before a city assumes that one will.

Both approaches also imply that maintenance belongs in the original design. Passage A’s movable chairs and planting beds remain advantages only if someone repairs, waters, and rearranges them. Passage B’s comparison of annual costs asks planners to identify that responsibility before construction. A neglected lot painted green for an opening ceremony would satisfy neither writer. For both, the physical size of the site is less decisive than the fit between a defined local need, an adaptable design, and evidence collected over enough time to show whether the space continues to serve people after its novelty fades.

Residents can contribute to that evidence without being reduced to a single satisfaction score. Short interviews may reveal why a bench remains empty, while timed observations show whether the report describes an occasional problem or a recurring one. A drainage test can complement both. Passage A would use such information to adapt the site; Passage B would also use it to judge whether continued spending on the site is preferable to another intervention. In each case, observation links a small physical space to the particular public purposes claimed for it.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
F) mocking and contemptuous
G) unqualified and triumphant
H) Passage A is pragmatic and encouraging; Passage B is skeptical but conditional.
J) panicked and accusatory

options.C: Passage A is pragmatic and encouraging; Passage B is skeptical but conditional.

questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

READING PASSAGE 4: Night Trains and City Heat
A city rail agency testing nighttime service noticed a pattern in electricity use. Trains consumed slightly more energy on the hottest nights, even when passenger counts were similar. Engineers first suspected the air-conditioning systems inside the cars. Measurements showed that those systems mattered, but they did not explain the entire increase.

Rails absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset. On warmer rails, electrical resistance rises slightly, and some trackside equipment requires more cooling. The effect for one train is small. Across hundreds of trips, however, small increases accumulate. The agency compared average energy per trip with the temperature measured at 10:00 p.m. for six test nights. The accompanying graph shows the results.

The data reveal an association, not a complete explanation. The hottest nights may also have different passenger patterns, delays, or wind conditions. To isolate the role of temperature, the agency plans to compare trains of the same model traveling the same route and stopping pattern. Engineers will also place sensors at shaded and unshaded track sections because air temperature alone may not represent rail temperature.

Even before that study is complete, the result can guide operations. Trains can be pre-cooled in the depot, where cooling equipment is more efficient, and nonessential trackside cabinets can be shaded. Neither step is expected to transform the system’s energy budget. The value lies in identifying several modest improvements that do not reduce service.

The next test will run for eight weeks rather than six selected nights. Each train will report energy used by propulsion, cabin cooling, and auxiliary systems separately. Track sensors will record rail temperature every five minutes, and dispatch records will identify delays. If energy remains associated with rail temperature after those factors are considered, the engineers will have a stronger basis for estimating the trackside contribution.

A different result would still be useful. If cabin cooling explains nearly all of the increase, the agency could focus on depot procedures rather than track equipment. In either case, the six-night graph has served its purpose: it has identified a pattern precise enough to investigate, but not precise enough to treat as a settled cause.

The agency will publish the follow-up data by trip rather than only as nightly averages. That choice will let analysts test whether a handful of delayed trains account for much of the increase. It will also reveal whether pre-cooling changes energy use at the depot, during the trip, or both. Riders are unlikely to notice any of these measurements, and that is part of the goal: the proposed adjustments preserve the same timetable and cabin comfort. The study treats efficiency as an accumulation of small operational choices, each supported by a pattern that survives a fair comparison.

Engineers will also compare nights with similar temperatures but different humidity and wind. Those variables can change how hard cooling equipment works and how quickly rails release stored heat. A result that weakens after these comparisons would not make the original graph erroneous; it would show that temperature had been standing in for a more complicated set of conditions. The follow-up study is designed precisely to discover whether the simple relationship remains useful after the hidden differences between nights are made visible.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
A) mocking and contemptuous
B) unqualified and triumphant
C) panicked and accusatory
D) analytical and appropriately tentative
questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

READING PASSAGE 1: The Last Drying Rack
For forty years, the print studio had dried paper on wooden racks that descended from the ceiling like narrow ladders. Lina knew each rack by its noises. Rack Three sighed when lowered. Rack Seven stopped two centimeters above the floor unless someone nudged its rope. The newest volunteers complained, reasonably, that the racks were awkward and slow.

A grant allowed the studio to buy rolling metal screens. They were clean, bright, and easy to rearrange. During installation, Lina labeled the old racks for removal. She felt no ceremony; equipment either served the work or it did not. Still, she postponed taking down Rack Seven because a class was using the wall beneath it.

That afternoon, a student named Dev printed a broad field of dark ink around a small unprinted circle. He had pressed too hard, and the paper carried a shallow ridge. On a flat screen the wet sheet sagged, allowing ink to pool along the ridge. Dev reached for another sheet, but Lina stopped him. She clipped the print to Rack Seven so that it hung vertically. Gravity drew the extra ink downward in thin, even paths. The mistake became a ring of lines around the white circle.

Dev asked whether the rack was designed for that effect. Lina nearly said yes. Instead, she explained that printers had long improvised with whatever the studio provided. The rack’s spacing, worn clips, and vertical drop could all leave marks. Most were flaws; a few became choices once the printer noticed them.

The next morning, Lina removed six old racks. She kept Rack Seven, but not as a monument. She mounted it lower, replaced its rope, and placed a card beside it: “Vertical drying rack. Slower than screens. Useful when gravity is part of the print.” Dev added a smaller handwritten note: “Ask the paper what falling can do.”

The studio looked larger with the other racks gone. The metal screens rolled neatly against one wall. Rack Seven no longer sighed or stuck. It remained because Lina had finally described its use precisely, not because she had refused to change.

Lina asked the next class to test the rack rather than accept the card as a rule. Students hung narrow test strips at different angles and used ink of two viscosities. Most combinations produced nothing worth keeping: blunt drips, pale edges, or paper that curled. A few created lines that could be repeated if clip position and ink thickness were recorded. Dev entered those conditions in a shared notebook.

The test did not make the rack indispensable. A future printer might find no reason to use it, and the studio could remove it when space changed again. For now, however, it occupied a defined place among the tools. The metal screens offered speed and consistency; the rack offered a controlled way to let motion continue after printing. Lina considered that distinction a better form of preservation than simply refusing to take old equipment down.

At the end of the term, Dev made two editions of the same image. One dried flat and retained a smooth black field; the other hung from Rack Seven and carried thin descending lines. He displayed them side by side without naming one correct and the other accidental. The difference lay in whether he had anticipated the movement and prepared the ink for it. Lina saw that the surviving rack had acquired a clearer purpose through the comparison. Its age had prompted the question, but a repeatable result—not age—had earned it space in the studio.

Other volunteers began applying the same rule to equipment stored elsewhere in the building. A heavy paper cutter remained because its alignment was unusually accurate; a cracked tray was photographed and discarded because no one could name a use that justified its leak. The conversations were sometimes difficult, but they replaced the broad categories of “old” and “new” with narrower questions about effect, safety, and repetition. Rack Seven had not won an exemption. It had helped the studio develop a better standard for change.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
F) observant, unsentimental, and quietly appreciative
G) mocking and contemptuous
H) unqualified and triumphant
J) panicked and accusatory
questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

READING PASSAGE 2: Restoring Kelp by Sound
A healthy kelp forest is not silent. Water moves through fronds, fish scrape algae from rocks, and invertebrates produce clicks and snaps. To a diver, many of these sounds blur into a faint crackle. To the larvae of some marine animals, however, the soundscape may provide information about where to settle.

This possibility has led restoration researchers to test underwater speakers near damaged reefs. A speaker plays recordings from a thriving habitat, and scientists compare the animals arriving near that speaker with those arriving near a silent control. In several studies, more juvenile fish appeared near the playback. The result suggests that sound can influence movement, but it does not show that every arriving animal will remain or that the habitat can support it.

Kelp restoration makes this limitation especially important. Young fish may be attracted to a recording, yet they still need shelter and food. If heat, pollution, or grazing has removed the kelp, sound alone cannot rebuild the physical habitat. Researchers therefore pair acoustic playback with other actions, such as planting juvenile kelp or reducing the number of grazing sea urchins.

The recordings themselves also require care. A reef varies by season and time of day. Boat engines can mask biological sounds, and a recording made close to one noisy species may not represent the habitat as a whole. Teams use several microphones, remove obvious equipment noise, and report the volume at which a recording is played. Excessive volume could attract animals from an unrealistically large area or disturb species the project intends to help.

Acoustic playback is best understood as one tool for testing and guiding recovery. If fish approach a restored plot more often when an appropriate soundscape is present, researchers can investigate whether the newcomers feed, grow, and remain. The method turns sound into a measurable part of habitat quality while keeping the larger requirement in view: a convincing invitation matters only if there is somewhere suitable to stay.

A long-term trial therefore follows more than arrival counts. Divers survey fish size and feeding behavior, cameras record how long individuals remain, and kelp measurements track canopy growth. Researchers may turn the speakers off after several weeks to learn whether any effect persists. If fish leave immediately, the sound may have acted only as a temporary cue. If they stay and use the restored habitat, playback may have helped a recovering community cross an early threshold.

The control sites are equally important. Natural recruitment can change from month to month, and a regional increase could make every plot look successful. Comparing silent and playback plots exposed to the same broader conditions helps separate that background variation from the effect of sound. The design does not make the ecosystem simple; it makes one proposed contribution testable.

The same caution applies when results are communicated to the public. A headline that says “sound restores reefs” compresses several uncertain steps into one claim. A more accurate description separates attraction, settlement, survival, and reproduction. Each can be measured on a different schedule and may respond to a different feature of the habitat. Researchers welcome interest in an unusual tool, but they also publish silent controls and unsuccessful trials. Those results reveal where playback stops being effective and where conventional restoration—water quality, grazing control, and kelp establishment—must do the essential work.

Site selection further complicates the work. A recording from a healthy forest may contain species that cannot live at the damaged site because depth, temperature, or current differs. Researchers therefore compare the source and restoration site before choosing a soundscape, and they may build a composite from several periods rather than loop one dramatic minute. The goal is not to make the site sound generically lively. It is to test cues that plausibly belong to the habitat the project is capable of supporting.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
A) mocking and contemptuous
B) explanatory and qualified
C) unqualified and triumphant
D) panicked and accusatory
questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

READING PASSAGE 3: A Map That Moves
A conventional bus map shows routes as fixed lines. For riders, however, the useful shape of a transit network changes through the day. A transfer that takes six minutes at noon may take eighteen minutes after evening service becomes less frequent. Researchers created a “time map” that redraws the distance between four stations according to median travel time rather than geographic distance.

The accompanying diagram shows the median minutes from Central Station to North, East, South, and West stations during midday and evening service. The geographic distance to each outer station is similar, but the time distances are not. East remains relatively close in both periods because two frequent routes serve it. West expands sharply in the evening, when one connecting route runs only every twenty minutes.

Such a map does not tell a rider exactly when a bus will arrive. Medians smooth over variation, and an unusually long delay may be hidden. The map also centers one starting point; a trip between two outer stations could have a different pattern. Its value is comparative. Planners can see which parts of the network become effectively farther away when frequency changes.

After reviewing the evening map, the agency tested shifting one bus from a lightly used downtown loop to the West connection after 7:00 p.m. The change reduced the median time to West without adding a bus to the fleet. The agency still examined crowding and on-time performance before making the change permanent. A map that moves is useful precisely because it invites a second question: what operational choice made the network stretch or shrink?

The designers also experimented with showing reliability. A thin band around each time distance represented the middle half of observed trips. East’s band remained narrow, while West’s evening band widened as well as lengthened. That addition warned planners that a median improvement could still leave some riders with unpredictable waits. It also prevented two routes with the same median from appearing equally dependable.

No single drawing could display every origin, time, and measure without becoming unreadable. The agency therefore treated the map as a view selected for a question, not a replacement for the schedule database. When the question concerned evening access from Central, the changing geometry made a hidden service gap visible. When the question concerned a rider’s exact trip, the underlying arrival data remained necessary.

Riders who reviewed early versions asked for one more feature: a switch between typical time and “leave by” time. The first described how long a trip usually took after boarding; the second included expected waiting. That distinction barely changed frequent East service but enlarged the evening West gap. The map did not become more geographically accurate. It became more faithful to the decision a rider was making. By letting the displayed distance depend on a clearly named measure, the designers made the apparent distortion interpretable rather than merely dramatic.

A later public version allowed riders to select a destination and watch the network redraw across four time periods. The animation made one point especially clear: a station could remain in the same place yet become harder to reach when transfers lengthened. Riders used the display to compare departure times; planners used it to locate abrupt changes created by schedules. Both groups still needed the ordinary map for streets and route names. The time map added a second geometry—one built from access rather than pavement.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
F) mocking and contemptuous
G) unqualified and triumphant
H) practical and analytical
J) panicked and accusatory
questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

READING PASSAGE 4: Museum Labels: Voice or Silence?
PASSAGE A
A museum label should give visitors a strong first foothold. A date, material, and place of origin can prevent avoidable confusion, but a useful label goes further. It may identify the choice an artist made, the problem a tool solved, or the reason an ordinary object survived. Brief interpretation does not close down looking; it gives visitors something specific to test against what they see.

Labels work best when they acknowledge uncertainty. “Probably used for cooking” invites a different kind of attention than “used for cooking.” A label can name competing explanations and tell visitors what evidence supports each one. The museum’s voice then becomes a guide to inquiry rather than a voice of final authority.

PASSAGE B
Visitors also need stretches of visual quiet. When a wall carries a paragraph beside every object, reading can become the default activity and looking a task performed afterward. Museums should experiment with fewer labels in selected rooms, while making deeper information available nearby or on request.

Silence is not neutral, of course. Without context, some objects become accessible only to visitors who already know their history. The solution is not to remove explanation everywhere. It is to design a rhythm: a clear introduction, room to observe, and optional layers for people who want more. A museum should not force every visitor to follow the same sequence of words before encountering an object.

Passage B proposes evaluating that rhythm with visitors who bring different levels of prior knowledge. In one trial, a room might provide a short entrance panel and optional labels placed slightly to the side; in another, every object might carry a standard paragraph. Researchers could observe where visitors pause, ask what they noticed, and check whether key context was available when wanted. The purpose would not be to find one universal density of words. It would be to identify when explanation opens attention and when it competes with it.

Such testing would also make the disagreement with Passage A narrower. Both writers reject labels that merely announce authority. Passage A concentrates on what a concise label can responsibly say; Passage B concentrates on where and when that voice should be present.

A layered system may also include audio, large print, translations, or tactile description. Optional does not mean hidden or difficult to request; the layers must be visible and usable. Passage B’s “rhythm” therefore involves access as well as visual calm, while Passage A’s concern for precise uncertainty applies in every format. A spoken guide should not sound more certain than the evidence allows, and a quiet wall should not force visitors to guess where context can be found. In both accounts, design choices shape who can begin an inquiry and how freely that inquiry can proceed.

Museums may also change the rhythm by object type. A familiar household tool can invite close looking before explanation, whereas a ceremonial object removed from its community may require immediate context to avoid a misleading interpretation. Neither passage supplies a formula for that decision. Instead, both treat labeling as an editorial act with consequences. Words can direct attention, disclose uncertainty, or crowd out observation; silence can create space, preserve ambiguity, or exclude. Responsible design begins by deciding which effect is intended in a particular room.

Which choice best describes the tone of the passage?
A) mocking and contemptuous
B) unqualified and triumphant
C) panicked and accusatory
D) Passage A is instructive; Passage B is cautionary but balanced.

options.D: Passage A is instructive; Passage B is cautionary but balanced.

questions.explanation: The author presents the subject with the measured attitude described in the correct choice.

Nora coordinated a public art exhibit that allowed residents to borrow specialized materials. At first, Nora assumed that adding more items would increase use. A short survey, however, showed that many visitors were uncertain about how to begin. The survey became a compass: it pointed the team toward clearer labels and a one-page guide. During the next month, completed loans rose from 26 to 35. Nora concluded that the collection had not needed to become larger; it had needed to become easier to navigate.

Caleb coordinated a library workshop that allowed residents to borrow specialized materials. At first, Caleb assumed that adding more items would increase use. A short survey, however, showed that many visitors were uncertain about how to begin. The survey became a compass: it pointed the team toward clearer labels and a one-page guide. During the next month, completed loans rose from 37 to 49. Caleb concluded that the collection had not needed to become larger; it had needed to become easier to navigate.

PASSAGE B
A second coordinator, Eli, agreed that instructions matter but argued that conversation is equally important. At Eli's site, volunteers greet new visitors and demonstrate one tool before explaining the catalog. Eli views the catalog as a reference, not a substitute for human guidance.

After revision: 49
